screens.title: The Role of Artifacts in Release Pipelines
screens.narratorSegment: At the heart of Continuous Delivery lies the seamless transition of software components from development to deployment. This is where artifacts and release pipelines become indispensable. An artifact is essentially a deployable component, the output of your Continuous Integration build, such as a compiled application package, a Docker image, or a set of configuration files. Release pipelines in Azure DevOps are designed to consume these artifacts and orchestrate their deployment to various target environments, like development, staging, or production. This integration is not just about moving files; it's about ensuring that the right, tested software components are delivered reliably and consistently. Without a robust artifact integration strategy, your deployments can become manual, error-prone, and difficult to scale. Think of it as the delivery truck for your software: it picks up the finished goods from the factory, which are your artifacts, and transports them safely to their destination, which are your environments. This systematic approach ensures that every deployment is based on a known, versioned set of components, drastically reducing the risk of 'it worked on my machine' scenarios. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. content.html:
Module 9›Chapter 9.8›Artifacts in Release Pipelines
Core Concept

The Role of Artifacts in Release Pipelines

Bridging CI builds to CD deployments for continuous delivery.

Artifacts are the deployable units: These are the outputs of your build pipelines, such as compiled code, Docker images, or configuration files, ready for deployment.

Release pipelines consume artifacts: They are designed to take these artifacts and automate their deployment to various target environments.

Ensures reliability and consistency: This integration guarantees that tested components are delivered predictably, reducing deployment risks.

Key Takeaway

Artifact integration is the cornerstone of Continuous Delivery, automating the journey of software components from build to deployment.

Analogy

The Software Delivery Truck

Imagine your CI build as a factory producing finished goods (artifacts). The release pipeline is the delivery truck that picks up these goods and transports them safely to various warehouses (environments). This systematic process ensures the right products reach the right destinations reliably.

Common Mistake

Manual Component Handling

Relying on manual copying or ad-hoc fetching of build outputs for deployments. This introduces human error, inconsistency, and makes rollbacks or audits extremely difficult. Always automate artifact consumption.

Why it matters

Ensuring Reproducibility

Proper artifact integration ensures that every deployment is based on a known, versioned set of components. This eliminates 'works on my machine' issues and guarantees that what was tested is exactly what gets deployed.

screens.title: Linking Artifacts: Azure Pipelines (Build Artifacts)
screens.narratorSegment: When you're setting up a new release pipeline in Azure DevOps, the very first step is to link the artifacts it will consume. The most common source for these artifacts is another Azure Pipeline, specifically your Continuous Integration or CI build pipeline. These are often referred to as 'build artifacts' and represent the direct output of your successful builds, such as compiled. zip files containing your web application, Docker image manifests, or even test reports. To link them, you simply specify which build pipeline produced the artifact. You then define the 'default version' – this could be the latest successful build, the latest from a specific branch, or a precise build number. A critical part of this process is assigning an 'artifact alias.' This is a human-readable name, like '_WebApp', that acts as a reference within your release pipeline. It makes it much easier to refer to the artifact in subsequent deployment tasks, ensuring clarity and maintainability. For example, if your CI pipeline builds a web application and publishes it as a 'drop-webapp' artifact, you would link this build pipeline and give it an alias like '_WebApp' in your release pipeline. This alias then becomes the logical name you use to access its contents during deployment.

content.html:
Module 9›Chapter 9.8›Linking Build Artifacts
Artifact Source

Linking Artifacts: Azure Pipelines

Connecting your CI build outputs to release pipelines.

Primary Source: Azure Pipelines: Most commonly, artifacts are the direct output of your CI builds, such as compiled `.zip` files or Docker image manifests.

Specify Build Pipeline & Version: You link to the specific build pipeline and define the default version (e.g., 'latest', 'latest from branch', or a 'specific build number').

Assign an Artifact Alias: A human-readable name (e.g., _WebApp) that simplifies referencing the artifact within your release pipeline tasks.

Key Takeaway

Linking Azure Pipelines artifacts involves selecting the source build, its version, and assigning a clear alias for easy reference in deployment tasks.

Example Scenario

Linking a Web App Build

Your CI pipeline WebApp-CI produces a webapp.zip artifact. In your release pipeline, you'd link WebApp-CI, set the default version to 'Latest', and assign the alias _WebApp. Now, _WebApp refers to the latest webapp.zip.

Common Mistake

Ambiguous Version Selection

Relying solely on 'Latest' for production deployments. While convenient for dev/test, it can lead to unexpected changes. For production, always pin to a 'Specific build number' for reproducibility.

Pro Tip

Meaningful Aliases

Use descriptive aliases like _FrontendApp, _BackendAPI, or _DatabaseScripts. This improves readability and makes your release pipeline easier to understand and maintain for your team.

screens.title: Linking Artifacts: Azure Artifacts & Repos
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond the direct outputs of your CI builds, Azure DevOps release pipelines offer the flexibility to consume artifacts from other crucial sources. One significant source is Azure Artifacts, which allows you to integrate packages directly from your feeds. This is incredibly useful for consuming shared libraries, pre-built components, or even Universal Packages that might not originate from your current build pipeline. You can specify the feed, the package type – such as NuGet, npm, Maven, or Universal Packages – the exact package name, and its default version. For instance, if your application relies on a common logging library published as a NuGet package in your 'MyOrgFeed', you can link directly to it. Another powerful option is linking directly to a GitHub or Azure Repos Git repository. While less common for compiled application artifacts, this is ideal for deploying configuration files, infrastructure-as-code templates, or scripts directly from source control. This ensures that your deployment logic and configuration are always in sync with your versioned repository. For example, you might link a repository containing environment-specific appsettings. json files, allowing your release pipeline to fetch the correct configuration for each deployment stage.

content.html:
Module 9›Chapter 9.8›Azure Artifacts & Repos
Artifact Source

Linking Artifacts: Azure Artifacts & Repos

Consuming packages and source control directly for diverse needs.

Azure Artifacts: Consume packages (NuGet, npm, Maven, Universal Packages) directly from your feeds. Ideal for shared libraries or pre-built components.

GitHub / Azure Repos: Link directly to a Git repository to fetch specific files, configuration, or Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) templates.

Specify Details: For Azure Artifacts, define feed, package type, name, and version. For repos, specify the repository and branch/commit.

Key Takeaway

Azure Artifacts and Git repositories provide flexible artifact sourcing for shared components, configurations, and IaC, complementing traditional build outputs.

Example Scenario

Consuming a Shared Library

Your application uses a common security library published as a NuGet package MyOrg.SecurityLib in your 'EnterpriseFeed'. You link this package, specifying its name and a stable version, ensuring your release pipeline always gets the correct dependency.

Common Mistake

Mixing Artifact Types Inappropriately

Using Git repos for large compiled binaries instead of build artifacts. While possible, it's less efficient and not designed for managing versioned deployable packages. Choose the source type that best fits the artifact's nature.

Pro Tip

Versioned Configurations

Store environment-specific configuration files (e.g., appsettings.json) in a Git repository. Link this repo to your release pipeline and fetch the appropriate files for each environment, ensuring configuration consistency and traceability.

screens.title: Linking Artifacts: External CI Systems
screens.narratorSegment: In many enterprise environments, you'll encounter hybrid setups where not all Continuous Integration processes run exclusively within Azure Pipelines. You might have existing build systems like Jenkins or TeamCity that produce critical artifacts. Azure DevOps release pipelines are designed with this reality in mind, offering robust integration capabilities for these external CI systems. This means you can still leverage the powerful deployment orchestration features of Azure DevOps, even if your builds are happening elsewhere. When linking an external artifact, you typically configure a service connection to your external CI system, such as a Jenkins server. You then specify the job or project within that system that produces the desired artifact. Azure DevOps will then be able to pull the build outputs from these external sources, treating them just like any other linked artifact. This flexibility is invaluable for organizations transitioning to Azure DevOps or those with complex, distributed build infrastructures. For example, if your legacy Java application is built by a Jenkins job that outputs a. war file, you can configure your Azure DevOps release pipeline to fetch that. war file directly from Jenkins, then deploy it to an Azure App Service or a virtual machine. This ensures a unified deployment experience regardless of where your builds originate.

Module 9›Chapter 9.8›External CI Integration
Artifact Source

Linking Artifacts: External CI Systems

Integrating Jenkins, TeamCity, and other build outputs for hybrid environments.

Hybrid Environment Support: Azure DevOps can integrate with external CI systems like Jenkins or TeamCity to consume their build outputs.

Service Connection Required: Typically involves configuring a service connection to the external system and specifying the relevant job or project.

Unified Deployment: This allows for a consistent deployment experience within Azure DevOps, regardless of where the initial build occurred.

Key Takeaway

Azure DevOps release pipelines can integrate with external CI systems, enabling unified deployment orchestration for hybrid build environments.

Example Scenario

Deploying a Jenkins-Built WAR File

Your legacy Java application is built by a Jenkins job, producing a my-app.war file. You configure an Azure DevOps service connection to Jenkins, link the Jenkins job, and then your release pipeline can fetch and deploy this .war file to an Azure App Service.

Common Mistake

Inadequate Permissions

The service connection to the external CI system lacks the necessary permissions to access and download artifacts. Always verify that the service principal or credentials used have 'read' access to the build outputs.

Pro Tip

Standardize Artifact Naming

Even with external systems, try to standardize artifact naming conventions. This makes it easier to configure the linking in Azure DevOps and ensures consistency across your entire artifact landscape.

screens.title: Defining Artifact Download Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Once you've linked your artifacts to a release pipeline, the next critical step is to define their download strategy. This dictates how and where these artifacts are fetched onto the deployment agent that will execute your tasks. By default, Azure Pipelines will download all linked artifacts to a specific directory on the agent, which is represented by the predefined variable $ open parenthesis Pipeline. Workspace close parenthesis. Each artifact will then be placed into its own subdirectory, named after the alias you assigned it. For example, if you linked a web application artifact with the alias '_WebApp', its contents would be downloaded to $ open parenthesis Pipeline. Workspace close parenthesis slash underscore Web App. This structured approach ensures that all your deployment tasks can easily locate and access the necessary files. However, you're not limited to the default behavior. You can customize this strategy, for instance, by choosing to download only specific artifacts if a job only needs a subset, or by skipping the download entirely if the artifact is already present on the agent from a previous run. This flexibility allows you to optimize agent disk space and download times, especially for large artifacts or frequent deployments. Understanding and configuring your download strategy is key to efficient and robust deployments, preventing issues like missing files or unnecessary data transfers.

keyIdea.text: Control how artifacts are downloaded to the agent's `$(Pipeline.Workspace)` directory, optimizing for specific needs.

content.html:
Module 9›Chapter 9.8›Download Strategies
Configuration

Defining Artifact Download Strategies

Controlling how artifacts are fetched to the agent for deployment.

Default Behavior: All linked artifacts are downloaded to the agent's $(Pipeline.Workspace) directory.

Alias-based Subdirectories: Each artifact is placed in a subdirectory named after its alias (e.g., $(Pipeline.Workspace)/_WebApp).

Customization Options: You can choose to download specific artifacts or skip downloads if already present, optimizing for performance and resource usage.

Key Takeaway

Artifact download strategies control where and how artifacts are fetched to the agent, using $(Pipeline.Workspace) and alias-based subdirectories for structured access.

Example Scenario

Targeted Artifact Download

Your release pipeline has _WebApp and _DBScripts artifacts. For a specific deployment job that only updates the database, you can configure it to download only _DBScripts, saving time and bandwidth by not fetching the web application.

Common Mistake

Assuming Artifact Location

Hardcoding paths to artifacts instead of using $(Pipeline.Workspace)/[ArtifactAlias]. This makes your pipeline fragile and prone to breaking if the agent's working directory changes or if you rename an alias.

Pro Tip

Use download: current

In YAML pipelines, use download: current at the job level to automatically download all linked artifacts to their default locations. This simplifies configuration and ensures all necessary components are present.

Workspace close parenthesis slash underscore Web App slash webapp. zip. You might then use a Power Shell@2 or Bash@3 task to unzip this file, or a dedicated Extract Files@1 task, preparing its contents for deployment. content.html:
Module 9›Chapter 9.8›Consuming Artifacts
Deployment Tasks

Utilizing Downloaded Artifacts in Deployment Jobs

Accessing artifact content for deployment tasks on the agent.

Artifacts become accessible: Once downloaded, artifacts are available to all tasks within the deployment job on the agent.

Pathing Convention: Always reference artifact content using $(Pipeline.Workspace)/[ArtifactAlias]/[FilePath].

Common Tasks: Use tasks like ExtractFiles@1, PowerShell@2, or Bash@3 to process artifact contents (e.g., unzip, copy).

Key Takeaway

Downloaded artifacts are accessed via $(Pipeline.Workspace)/[Alias], enabling deployment tasks to process and deploy their contents reliably.

Example Scenario

Unzipping a Web Application

If _WebApp contains webapp.zip, you'd use Expand-Archive -Path "$(Pipeline.Workspace)/_WebApp/webapp.zip" -DestinationPath "$(Agent.TempDirectory)/WebAppContent" in a PowerShell task to extract its contents.

Common Mistake

Incorrect Pathing

Referencing artifacts using absolute paths or incorrect variable names. Always use the `$(Pipeline.Workspace)` variable combined with the artifact alias to ensure portability and avoid runtime errors.

Pro Tip

Leverage Agent Temp Directory

For intermediate processing, like unzipping, use $(Agent.TempDirectory). This provides a clean, temporary workspace for files that don't need to persist beyond the current job execution.

screens.title: Managing Artifact Versions and Avoiding Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Effective artifact management extends beyond just linking and downloading; it's also about ensuring reproducibility and avoiding common pitfalls. A critical best practice is to always use specific versions for your releases, especially for production deployments. While selecting 'latest' might seem convenient for development or testing environments, it introduces variability, meaning you might deploy something different than what was tested. Pinning to a specific build number or package version guarantees that you are deploying exactly what was approved and validated. Another common mistake to avoid is hardcoding paths to artifacts within your deployment scripts. Always use the $ open parenthesis Pipeline. Workspace close parenthesis slash open square bracket Artifact Alias close square bracket pattern. This ensures portability and correctness, as the exact location on the agent can vary. Furthermore, ensure that the service connection used for downloading Azure Artifacts has the necessary 'Reader' permissions on the target feed. Without these permissions, your pipeline will fail to fetch the required packages. By adhering to these practices, you significantly enhance the reliability and auditability of your release process, making it easier to troubleshoot and roll back if necessary. Remember, consistency and explicit versioning are your allies in robust Continuous Delivery.

keyIdea.text: Always use specific artifact versions, avoid hardcoding paths, and ensure correct permissions for reliable releases.

content.html:
Module 9›Chapter 9.8›Versioning & Pitfalls
Best Practices

Managing Artifact Versions and Avoiding Pitfalls

Ensuring reproducibility and correctness in deployments.

Use Specific Versions: For production, always pin to a specific build number or package version to ensure reproducibility and stability.

Avoid Hardcoding Paths: Always use $(Pipeline.Workspace)/[ArtifactAlias] to reference artifact content, ensuring portability.

Verify Permissions: Ensure service connections for Azure Artifacts have 'Reader' permissions on the target feed to prevent download failures.

Key Takeaway

Adhering to specific versioning, dynamic pathing, and correct permissions are crucial best practices for robust and reproducible artifact management in release pipelines.

Example Scenario

Pinning a Production Release

For your production release, instead of selecting 'Latest' for the _WebApp artifact, you explicitly choose 'Build 20231026.5'. This guarantees that the exact web application version that passed all tests is deployed, preventing unexpected behavior.

Common Mistake

Missing Feed Permissions

A release pipeline fails to download a NuGet package from Azure Artifacts. The common cause is that the service connection used by the pipeline's agent lacks 'Reader' permissions on the specific Azure Artifacts feed.

Pro Tip

Audit Trails

Using specific versions for artifacts creates a clear audit trail. You can easily trace back which exact components were deployed in any given release, which is invaluable for compliance and debugging.

screens.title: Leveraging Azure Artifacts Views for Quality
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond simply pinning to specific versions, Azure Artifacts offers a powerful feature called 'views' to further enhance quality assurance in your release pipelines. Views allow you to create logical subsets of packages within a feed, often used to gate packages based on their quality or approval status. For instance, you might have a '@local' view for packages still under development, a '@beta' view for packages undergoing internal testing, and a '@release' view for packages that have passed all quality gates and are approved for production. When configuring your release pipeline to consume artifacts from an Azure Artifacts feed, you can specify not just the package name and version, but also the specific view. This is incredibly powerful for production deployments. By configuring a production release pipeline to only consume packages from the '@release' view, you guarantee that only fully vetted and approved components are ever deployed to your most critical environments. This adds an additional, robust layer of control and quality assurance to your deployment process, preventing accidental deployments of untested or unapproved packages. It's a strategic way to manage the lifecycle of your packages and ensure that only high-quality, stable components make it to your end-users.

content.html:
Module 9›Chapter 9.8›Artifact Views
Advanced Configuration

Leveraging Azure Artifacts Views for Quality

Gating packages for production deployments and ensuring quality assurance.

Logical Subsets: Views create logical subsets of packages within an Azure Artifacts feed, categorizing them by quality or approval status.

Quality Gating: Use views like @release to ensure only fully vetted and approved packages are considered for production deployments.

Enhanced Control: Provides an additional layer of control and quality assurance, preventing accidental deployments of untested packages.

Key Takeaway

Azure Artifacts views are a powerful mechanism for quality gating, ensuring that only approved and stable packages are consumed by production release pipelines.

Example Scenario

Production Release with Views

Your production release pipeline is configured to consume MyOrg.CoreLib from 'MyOrgFeed' at version '1.0.0@release'. This ensures that only the 1.0.0 package that has been explicitly promoted to the @release view is deployed, guaranteeing its quality.

Common Mistake

Ignoring Views for Critical Environments

Not utilizing views for production or critical environments. This leaves a loophole where untested packages could inadvertently be deployed if they share the same version number but haven't passed quality gates.

Pro Tip

Automate View Promotion

Integrate view promotion into your CI/CD process. Once a package passes all automated tests and approvals, automatically promote it to the next view (e.g., from @beta to @release) to streamline the quality gating process.

Welcome to this crucial chapter on integrating artifacts with release pipelines in Azure DevOps. In the world of Continuous Delivery, successfully building your software is only half the battle. The other, equally vital half, is ensuring that the right software components, or artifacts, are reliably delivered to your target environments. This chapter will guide you through the process of connecting the outputs of your build pipelines to your release pipelines, forming the backbone of automated deployments. We'll explore how to link various artifact types, configure their download strategies, and effectively utilize them within your deployment jobs. Understanding this integration is fundamental to achieving robust, repeatable, and efficient software delivery, allowing you to confidently move your applications from development to production. By the end of this session, you'll have a clear understanding of how to orchestrate your deployments using artifacts, making your DevOps workflow seamless and reliable.

In this chapter, our primary goal is to equip you with the skills to effectively integrate artifacts into your Azure DevOps release pipelines. First, you will learn to understand and differentiate between various types of artifacts, such as compiled build outputs, packages from Azure Artifacts, or even external sources, and how to link them correctly to your release pipelines. This foundational knowledge is crucial for setting up any deployment. Next, we'll dive into configuring artifact aliases and defining efficient download strategies. This ensures that your deployment agents retrieve exactly what they need, optimizing performance and resource usage. Finally, you'll gain practical experience in utilizing these downloaded artifacts within your deployment jobs and tasks, transforming raw components into deployed applications. These objectives are designed to give you a comprehensive understanding of artifact management, a cornerstone of robust Continuous Delivery.

Building on our foundational understanding, this screen outlines further key objectives to deepen your expertise in artifact integration. You will learn to implement best practices for managing artifact versions and sources within your release pipelines, which is critical for maintaining stability and reproducibility across environments. We'll also explore how to apply YAML snippets for artifact consumption directly within your deployment jobs, giving you practical, code-based skills. Furthermore, you'll learn to identify and avoid common mistakes related to artifact pathing and permissions, preventing frustrating deployment failures. Finally, we'll cover how to strategically use version pinning and Azure Artifacts views to ensure that only quality-gated packages are considered for deployment, adding an essential layer of quality assurance to your release process. These advanced objectives will solidify your ability to manage artifacts with confidence and precision.

At the heart of Continuous Delivery lies the seamless transition of software components from development to deployment. This is where artifacts and release pipelines become indispensable. An artifact is essentially a deployable component, the output of your Continuous Integration build, such as a compiled application package, a Docker image, or a set of configuration files. Release pipelines in Azure DevOps are designed to consume these artifacts and orchestrate their deployment to various target environments, like development, staging, or production. This integration is not just about moving files; it's about ensuring that the right, tested software components are delivered reliably and consistently. Without a robust artifact integration strategy, your deployments can become manual, error-prone, and difficult to scale. Think of it as the delivery truck for your software: it picks up the finished goods from the factory, which are your artifacts, and transports them safely to their destination, which are your environments. This systematic approach ensures that every deployment is based on a known, versioned set of components, drastically reducing the risk of 'it worked on my machine' scenarios. The Role of Artifacts in Release Pipelines means artifacts are the deployable outputs of ci, consumed by release pipelines for automated, reliable deployments.. In practical terms, bridging ci builds to cd deployments for continuous delivery.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When you're setting up a new release pipeline in Azure DevOps, the very first step is to link the artifacts it will consume. The most common source for these artifacts is another Azure Pipeline, specifically your Continuous Integration or CI build pipeline. These are often referred to as 'build artifacts' and represent the direct output of your successful builds, such as compiled. zip files containing your web application, Docker image manifests, or even test reports. To link them, you simply specify which build pipeline produced the artifact. You then define the 'default version' – this could be the latest successful build, the latest from a specific branch, or a precise build number. A critical part of this process is assigning an 'artifact alias.' This is a human-readable name, like '_WebApp', that acts as a reference within your release pipeline. It makes it much easier to refer to the artifact in subsequent deployment tasks, ensuring clarity and maintainability. For example, if your CI pipeline builds a web application and publishes it as a 'drop-webapp' artifact, you would link this build pipeline and give it an alias like '_WebApp' in your release pipeline. This alias then becomes the logical name you use to access its contents during deployment.

Beyond the direct outputs of your CI builds, Azure DevOps release pipelines offer the flexibility to consume artifacts from other crucial sources. One significant source is Azure Artifacts, which allows you to integrate packages directly from your feeds. This is incredibly useful for consuming shared libraries, pre-built components, or even Universal Packages that might not originate from your current build pipeline. You can specify the feed, the package type – such as NuGet, npm, Maven, or Universal Packages – the exact package name, and its default version. For instance, if your application relies on a common logging library published as a NuGet package in your 'MyOrgFeed', you can link directly to it. Another powerful option is linking directly to a GitHub or Azure Repos Git repository. While less common for compiled application artifacts, this is ideal for deploying configuration files, infrastructure-as-code templates, or scripts directly from source control. This ensures that your deployment logic and configuration are always in sync with your versioned repository. For example, you might link a repository containing environment-specific appsettings. json files, allowing your release pipeline to fetch the correct configuration for each deployment stage.

In many enterprise environments, you'll encounter hybrid setups where not all Continuous Integration processes run exclusively within Azure Pipelines. You might have existing build systems like Jenkins or TeamCity that produce critical artifacts. Azure DevOps release pipelines are designed with this reality in mind, offering robust integration capabilities for these external CI systems. This means you can still leverage the powerful deployment orchestration features of Azure DevOps, even if your builds are happening elsewhere. When linking an external artifact, you typically configure a service connection to your external CI system, such as a Jenkins server. You then specify the job or project within that system that produces the desired artifact. Azure DevOps will then be able to pull the build outputs from these external sources, treating them just like any other linked artifact. This flexibility is invaluable for organizations transitioning to Azure DevOps or those with complex, distributed build infrastructures. For example, if your legacy Java application is built by a Jenkins job that outputs a. war file, you can configure your Azure DevOps release pipeline to fetch that. war file directly from Jenkins, then deploy it to an Azure App Service or a virtual machine. This ensures a unified deployment experience regardless of where your builds originate.

Once you've linked your artifacts to a release pipeline, the next critical step is to define their download strategy. This dictates how and where these artifacts are fetched onto the deployment agent that will execute your tasks. By default, Azure Pipelines will download all linked artifacts to a specific directory on the agent, which is represented by the predefined variable $ open parenthesis Pipeline. Workspace close parenthesis. Each artifact will then be placed into its own subdirectory, named after the alias you assigned it. For example, if you linked a web application artifact with the alias '_WebApp', its contents would be downloaded to $ open parenthesis Pipeline. Workspace close parenthesis slash underscore Web App. This structured approach ensures that all your deployment tasks can easily locate and access the necessary files. However, you're not limited to the default behavior. You can customize this strategy, for instance, by choosing to download only specific artifacts if a job only needs a subset, or by skipping the download entirely if the artifact is already present on the agent from a previous run. This flexibility allows you to optimize agent disk space and download times, especially for large artifacts or frequent deployments. Understanding and configuring your download strategy is key to efficient and robust deployments, preventing issues like missing files or unnecessary data transfers.

Workspace close parenthesis directory, they become fully accessible to all subsequent deployment tasks within that job. This is where the rubber meets the road, as you'll use these artifacts to perform the actual deployment actions. Effective artifact management extends beyond just linking and downloading; it's also about ensuring reproducibility and avoiding common pitfalls. A critical best practice is to always use specific versions for your releases, especially for production deployments. While selecting 'latest' might seem convenient for development or testing environments, it introduces variability, meaning you might deploy something different than what was tested. Pinning to a specific build number or package version guarantees that you are deploying exactly what was approved and validated. Furthermore, ensure that the service connection used for downloading Azure Artifacts has the necessary 'Reader' permissions on the target feed. Without these permissions, your pipeline will fail to fetch the required packages. By adhering to these practices, you significantly enhance the reliability and auditability of your release process, making it easier to troubleshoot and roll back if necessary. Remember, consistency and explicit versioning are your allies in robust Continuous Delivery.

Beyond simply pinning to specific versions, Azure Artifacts offers a powerful feature called 'views' to further enhance quality assurance in your release pipelines. Views allow you to create logical subsets of packages within a feed, often used to gate packages based on their quality or approval status. For instance, you might have a '@local' view for packages still under development, a '@beta' view for packages undergoing internal testing, and a '@release' view for packages that have passed all quality gates and are approved for production. When configuring your release pipeline to consume artifacts from an Azure Artifacts feed, you can specify not just the package name and version, but also the specific view. This is incredibly powerful for production deployments. By configuring a production release pipeline to only consume packages from the '@release' view, you guarantee that only fully vetted and approved components are ever deployed to your most critical environments. This adds an additional, robust layer of control and quality assurance to your deployment process, preventing accidental deployments of untested or unapproved packages. It's a strategic way to manage the lifecycle of your packages and ensure that only high-quality, stable components make it to your end-users.

Let's recap some of the essential concepts we've covered in this chapter. Next, we have Artifact Linking, which is the crucial process of associating these build outputs or packages from diverse sources with your release pipeline. This step tells the pipeline what components it needs to deploy. Finally, the Artifact Alias is a human-readable name you assign to a linked artifact. This alias is vital because it provides a clear, consistent way to reference the artifact's content within your release pipeline's jobs and tasks, making your scripts more readable and maintainable. Understanding these three concepts is fundamental to building robust and efficient deployment workflows.
